prize_parts.citation: for an uncompromising body of experimental fiction in Chinese that dissolves the boundary between inner and outer worlds and reinvents the possibilities of the narrative imagination

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading my colleagues. Can Xue has one of the most recognizable voices on the list. Her dreamlike, non-causal fiction (Frontier; Love in the New Millennium, with many earlier stories and novels) breaks with conventional psychology, space and causality. It is also not a single-book effect: the formal commitment runs over several decades. Her work is often placed beside Kafka and Borges, but the logic of the fiction is her own and is made in Chinese. The case rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal radicalism and imaginative depth across the whole oeuvre. It does not rest on fame, nationality or symbolism. The attribution is clean: one writer, one sustained project, and a citation that fits the whole body of work rather than one title.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one several colleagues raised, and I share it. The method is so consistent from book to book that it may deepen or may harden into a recurring procedure. I cannot settle that from the representative works and partial translations alone. A second concern is that the prose is deliberately opaque and reaches us through few translators, so my judgment of linguistic achievement is partly a judgment of those translations. If the committee finds that the late work only repeats the earlier mode, Cărtărescu's cumulative architecture would be the stronger whole-oeuvre case.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Michon first for the language-centered, compressed achievement of his prose. She also doubts whether the scale and self-referential density of Cărtărescu's later books sustain themselves, and she asks whether Can Xue's consistent dream logic shows development.
responses.response: I take the repetition question about Can Xue seriously. My answer is that consistency of method is not by itself a lack of depth. What matters is whether each book re-examines perception and selfhood or only restages them, and I accept that this is not fully verifiable from translations. On Michon, I agree that the sentence-level achievement is outstanding. But a prize for a whole body of work asks about breadth as well as intensity, and a small oeuvre with a narrow thematic range is a real limit for me. I read Mattson's doubt about Cărtărescu's length as the same kind of question I ask of Can Xue, so I do not think it separates them clearly.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first. He sees a poetic project of rare formal and conceptual ambition that turns dictatorship-era suffering into collective memorial form, with a voice sustained across decades.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson about Zurita's ambition and about the unmistakable voice, and I ranked him fourth for that reason. My hesitation is the one Olsson himself states: the landscape and sky interventions are known mainly through documentation, and poetry travels worst in translation. So I am less sure than he is that the whole project can be weighed as literature. I would want a citation resting on the poems themselves, not on historical symbolism. That is why I put the more text-centred case of Can Xue ahead of him.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first, as a visionary prose project whose large late works extend rather than repeat the earlier ones. He ranks Can Xue third, with the risk of repeated procedure that cannot be settled without close reading.
responses.response: I agree that the risk of repeated procedure is the central question about Can Xue, and I do not want to wave it away. I also accept that Cărtărescu's late books are described as extending his earlier work, which is a point in his favour. But I cannot confirm development in either corpus from public knowledge, and the longest Cărtărescu volumes run the opposite risk of excess. For me the two remain close, and I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative. What tips my preference to Can Xue is the radical break with realist psychology, which no other candidate here achieves as completely.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first for the unity and scale of a visionary project. She flags that his dense Romanian prose depends heavily on translation and that coverage of his poetry and early work is thinner.
responses.response: I agree that the case for Cărtărescu rests on the unity and scale of the project, and I agree that his linguistic achievement is hard to judge in translation. That uncertainty applies at least as strongly to Can Xue, whose oblique prose also depends on a small number of translators, so I do not think translation risk favours either of them. Carlberg ranks NDiaye fourth with real appreciation of her formal restraint, and I keep NDiaye as a second alternative for that reason. My remaining difference with Carlberg is about weighting, not about facts: I value Can Xue's uncompromising break with causal narrative above the encyclopedic scale of Cărtărescu.

uncertainties: Only part of Can Xue's large output is available in translation, and I cannot independently verify translation quality or how the later books relate to the earlier ones.
Whether her consistent method keeps developing or has become a recurring procedure is not settled by the evidence supplied to me.
Comparison across languages and genres (Chinese fiction, Romanian prose, Spanish poetry, French fiction, Arabic poetry) depends on translations, so rankings between them carry real uncertainty.
My assessments rest on general public knowledge of the works and on the opening statements, not on fresh reading or independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I serve on the committee with the other members and was elected to the Academy in the same renewal round as Ellen Mattson, but these are ordinary collegial ties and give no sign of a connection to any shortlisted writer.
